questions.title: Is the entropy definition missing a minus sign in BLT’s patching criterion?
questions.question_body:
In Section 2.3 (Entropy Patching), the paper defines the next-byte entropy as

$$H(x_i) = \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}} p_e(x_i=v\mid \mathbf{x}_{<i}) \log p_e(x_i=v\mid \mathbf{x}_{<i})$$

This is typically negative unless there is an explicit minus sign or a specified log base with negation. Later, the method thresholds entropy with conditions like $H(x_t) > \theta_g$. Should the definition actually be $H(x_i) = -\sum_v p_e \log p_e$? Also, what log base is used and how are the threshold values (e.g., $\theta_g=0.6$ vs $0.1$ during inference) calibrated under that convention?

questions.title: How does entropy-based patching remain incremental at generation time?
questions.question_body: The paper states that patching must be incremental for generation, i.e., it must decide a boundary at position $i$ without seeing future bytes and must satisfy $f_p(\mathbf{x}_{<i}) = f_p(\mathbf{x})_{<i}$. For entropy-based patching, the boundary decision depends on $H(x_i)$ computed by a small byte LM. During generation, is this entropy computed autoregressively using only the generated prefix? Does this require running a separate LM in parallel at every step, and how are the extra FLOPs accounted for? If not, what approximation is used to make the boundary decision online?

questions.title: Why do the authors claim BPE is not incremental—aren’t most practical BPE tokenizers left-to-right greedy and prefix-deterministic?
questions.question_body: Section 2.4 claims that BPE is not an incremental patching scheme because the same prefix can be tokenized differently depending on the continuation, i.e., it may violate $f_p(\mathbf{x}_{<i}) = f_p(\mathbf{x})_{<i}$. However, many BPE/WordPiece-style tokenizers used in LLMs implement greedy longest-match left-to-right tokenization that is prefix-deterministic. Can the authors clarify which tokenizer variant or training/inference setting makes BPE non-incremental in their claim, and provide a concrete counterexample where a standard GPT-style BPE produces different segmentations for the same prefix depending on the continuation?

questions.title: Clarifying the FLOPs-per-byte equation for BLT: what do m, r, and k refer to exactly?
questions.question_body:
In Section 3.6 (FLOPs Estimation), the FLOPs per byte for BLT is summarized as a sum over Transformer and Cross-Attention terms with arguments like $m$, $r$, $k$, and $V$. For example, the first term uses $\text{Transf. FL}(h_{\mathcal{G}}, l_{\mathcal{G}}, m=n_{ctx}/n_p, V=0)/n_p$, and cross-attn terms scale with $r$ and $k/n_p$. Could you provide a concrete worked example (with numbers) explaining:
- Why $m$ for the global Transformer is set to $n_{ctx}/n_p$ and then divided by $n_p$.
- How $k$ (the number of local splits concatenated) impacts cross-attention FLOPs and why the factor $\times k/n_p$ appears.
- How $r$ (query-to-key/value ratio) is computed for encoder vs. decoder cross-attn.
- How these terms change when average patch size increases from 4.5 to 8 bytes.

questions.title: Does cross-attention in the encoder restrict patches from leveraging left context outside the patch?
questions.question_body: The local encoder first runs a local self-attention with a sliding window of $w_{\mathcal{E}}$ bytes (which can cross patch boundaries), and then uses a cross-attention where each patch query only attends to the bytes inside the patch. Since the patch query is initialized by pooling the encoder byte representations, do patch representations still indirectly incorporate left-context information beyond the patch through those byte representations? Is the pooling done after the encoder has already mixed left-context into $h_{l-1,i}$, effectively allowing the patch vector to carry context beyond its own byte span despite the restricted cross-attn mask?

questions.title: Why are hash n-gram embeddings limited to n=3..8, and how severe are collisions at 500k hashes?
questions.question_body: Section 2.2 introduces hash n-gram embeddings for $n \in \{3,4,5,6,7,8\}$. Why exclude $n=1$ or $n=2$ grams, which might capture useful short-range orthographic signals? Also, with 500k hash buckets over all $n$-gram tables (or per $n$?), what is the expected collision rate for typical English and code corpora? Do collisions help as a regularizer, or do they hurt on structured domains (e.g., code)? Any empirical collision analysis would be helpful.

questions.title: How exactly are patch queries initialized and projected to the global dimension in the encoder cross-attention?
questions.question_body:
In Section 2.2.2, patch queries $P_{0,j}$ are initialized by pooling the byte embeddings of patch $p_j$ and then applying a linear projection $\mathcal{E}_C$. The text notes that patch representations are typically of dimension $h_{\mathcal{G}}$ whereas byte representations are $h_{\mathcal{E}}$, and that multihead outputs are concatenated later. Could you detail the tensor shapes through the cross-attention operation? Specifically:
- What is the shape of $P_{0,j}$ after pooling and $\mathcal{E}_C$?
- Are $Q$, $K$, $V$ in $\mathbb{R}^{U \times d_k}$ per head with $Ud_k = h_{\mathcal{G}}$ or $h_{\mathcal{E}}$?
- At what step are the multiple encoder heads concatenated to reach $h_{\mathcal{G}}$?

questions.title: How is causal correctness enforced when decoding bytes from patch representations?
questions.question_body: In the local decoder, the decoder first performs cross-attention from byte queries to patch keys/values, then applies a decoder Transformer layer. Since patches summarize multiple future bytes within the same patch, how do you ensure that decoding remains strictly autoregressive at the byte level? Is the cross-attention restricted so that byte position $i$ can only attend to patch information consistent with bytes $\le i$? Or do you rely on the fact that $o_j$ is produced by a global autoregressive model at the patch level, and the local decoder only conditions on the current patch representation and the previously generated bytes, thereby preserving causality?

questions.title: Reconciling ‘equalizing context length’ with ‘packing the same number of patches per batch’ during training
questions.question_body: Section 3.3 says you equalize the number of bytes per batch across patching schemes to avoid granting longer-patch models an unfair advantage. But it also says that, for efficiency, training packs batches of patches so every batch has the same number of patches, padding/truncating byte sequences to 12k/24k bytes to avoid memory spikes. How do these two batching rules interact in practice? If the number of patches per batch is fixed, doesn’t that implicitly favor smaller patches (more bytes per batch) or vice versa? A concrete example of how a mixed corpus batch is formed under entropy patching vs. space patching would help.

questions.title: What is ‘entropy drift’ and why does resetting the entropy context at newlines help?
questions.question_body:
In Section 3.5, you mention that entropy patching yields larger patches in repetitive contexts (e.g., multiple-choice formats) and that this variation is caused by lower entropy due to content repeated in the small LM’s context. You mitigate this by resetting the entropy model’s context at newlines and using the approximate-monotonicity constraint. Could you explain:
- How entropy drift manifests quantitatively (e.g., does average $H(x_i)$ systematically decrease over long repetitive regions)?
- Why newline resets are a good proxy for context boundaries that reduce drift?
- How the monotonicity-based boundary rule interacts with a reset to stabilize average patch size?

questions.title: How does the approximate monotonicity constraint for entropy patching segment a sequence algorithmically?
questions.question_body:
You present two boundary rules: a global threshold $H(x_t) > \theta_g$ and a relative/monotonic rule $H(x_t) - H(x_{t-1}) > \theta_r$. Could you detail the full segmentation algorithm for the monotonic rule? For instance:
- Do you always start a new patch when the relative increase exceeds $\theta_r$, regardless of patch length so far?
- Is there a minimum or maximum patch length enforced?
- How do you tune $\theta_r$ to hit a target average patch size on a given training mix?

questions.title: What is the exact attention mask for the global latent transformer (‘block-causal’) at the patch level?
questions.question_body: Section 2.1 states the global transformer uses a block-causal attention mask, restricting attention up to and including the current patch within the document. Does that mean patch $j$ can attend to all patch-level keys/values from patches $\le j$ within the same document (full prefix attention), and zero across documents? If patches vary in length across sequences, do you additionally pad and mask within a batch so that each sequence’s patch prefix is respected independently? A brief schematic of the patch-level mask would be helpful.

questions.title: Do the FLOPs estimates account for FlexAttention overheads and dynamic masks in practice?
questions.question_body: The theoretical FLOPs follow Chinchilla-style formulas and assume efficient implementations; however, for dynamic patch-dependent masks you rely on FlexAttention rather than FlashAttention. Do the reported flop-controlled scaling trends use theoretical FLOPs only, or do they reflect wall-clock-normalized FLOPs (accounting for kernel fusion, mask generation, and launch overhead)? If not, how large are the deviations in practice between theoretical and effective throughput for BLT vs. BPE baselines?

questions.title: How can a small-context entropy model be turned into a ‘lookup table’?
questions.question_body: Section 3.2 claims that when the receptive field of the entropy model is small enough, it can be encoded into an efficient lookup table. Given the byte alphabet size 256, even a context of length 6 yields $256^6$ states, which is infeasible. What exactly is being looked up? Are contexts hashed into a much smaller table (with collisions), or are you memoizing model outputs over a fixed training corpus? Some detail on the representation and collision/approximation behavior would clarify this claim.

questions.title: When adjusting the entropy threshold at inference (0.6 → 0.1), how do you avoid train–test compute mismatch issues?
questions.question_body: In Table 4, the BLT-Entropy model reduces the entropy threshold at inference from $0.6$ to $0.1$ to improve task performance at the cost of more steps. Does this change create a significant distribution shift between training and inference in terms of average patch size and the frequency of invoking the global transformer? If so, how do you ensure stability and calibration (e.g., LM head logits, layernorm stats) under lower thresholds at inference?

questions.title: How is causality preserved across patches when the local encoder uses a sliding window that can cross patch boundaries?
questions.question_body: The local encoder’s attention window can cross patch boundaries to incorporate nearby left context. When the global model processes patch $j$, its query is derived from encoder states whose receptive field potentially includes bytes from previous patches. Is this equivalent to standard autoregressive conditioning at the patch level, or does it risk leaking information from patch $j$+1 back into $j$ via the encoder? A precise statement of the causal masking guarantees in the encoder would help.

questions.title: How do you align RoPE and other architectural hyperparameters when initializing BLT’s global transformer from Llama 3.1?
questions.question_body: In Section 5.2, BLT initializes the global transformer from a pre-trained Llama 3.1 and then trains with 0.1× LR on the global layers. Since BLT’s global transformer runs at the patch level (not tokens), does the RoPE configuration (e.g., base $\theta$) directly transfer without mismatch in effective position scaling? If the patch counts and positional ranges differ from token positions, are any rescaling or interpolation steps applied to RoPE, and do those affect stability or downstream performance?

questions.title: Are comparisons to SpaceByte and MegaByte strictly apples-to-apples given cross-attention and hash embeddings?
questions.question_body: Some ablations compare BLT variants against SpaceByte- or MegaByte-like baselines. In a few places you note earlier runs lacked cross-attention, or that hash n-gram embeddings materially improve performance. Could you clarify which comparisons are strictly architecture-matched except for the patching scheme, and which include additional BLT components (e.g., cross-attn, hash embeddings) that SpaceByte/MegaByte did not have? A summary table labeling which knobs are on/off per baseline would reduce ambiguity.

questions.title: How is BPB computed and compared fairly across tokenized vs. byte models on mixed-domain corpora?
questions.question_body: Bits per byte (BPB) is used as a tokenizer-independent metric. When evaluating BPB on a subset of the pretraining mix, do all models score the exact same raw byte sequences and lengths, with identical document boundaries and normalization (e.g., UTF-8 validity, newline normalization)? Are there any pre-processing differences (like de-duplication, filtering) that could skew BPB across domains (CommonCrawl, Wikipedia, GitHub)? A short protocol for BPB evaluation parity would be helpful.

questions.title: What exactly are ‘space-like’ bytes, and how does Space Patching behave on non-Latin scripts?
questions.question_body: Section 2.2 defines space-like bytes as any byte that is not a Latin character, digit, or UTF-8 continuation byte, with at least one non-space-like byte per patch. This seems to treat many non-Latin scripts (which may encode characters over multiple bytes) as boundaries too frequently. Could you provide examples of segmentations for common non-Latin scripts (e.g., Devanagari, Arabic, Chinese in UTF-8)? How does this heuristic avoid pathological over-segmentation in multilingual data?

questions.title: Scaling intuition: why do larger patch sizes lag at small scale but catch up (or surpass) at larger scales?
questions.question_body: The paper notes that BLT with larger average patch sizes (e.g., 8 bytes) starts off worse than BPE or smaller patches at ~1B parameters but then closes the gap or surpasses BPE as the global model scales to 7–8B. Can you provide a more formal or empirical rationale? For instance, are local encoder/decoder FLOPs/params sublinear in total scale so that global model capacity becomes the bottleneck and benefits more from longer patches? Any plots of FLOPs breakdown by module vs. model size would help ground this intuition.
